title: The Volcano That Blew Its Own Top Off: Tambora 1815
description:
Unreal but true: a new real event every day at 5:48 pm (Riyadh).

In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia, had the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history (VEI 7). Before it, the mountain stood about 4,300 m high. Afterwards it was only 2,851 m: about 1,450 m, roughly a third of its height, was gone, leaving a caldera 6 to 7 km across. That is more than three Empire State Buildings (443 m each, to the tip) stacked up. About 10,000 people were killed directly, and tens of thousands more died of famine and disease afterwards (estimates range from at least 71,000 to more than 90,000 in total). The ash and gas cooled the planet, and 1816 became known as "the year without a summer".

The heights are to scale; the mountain's width is not, and the timing is not real time.

Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Mount Tambora" (about 4,300 m before, 2,851 m now, a caldera about 6 km across, at least 10,000 killed directly and some 80,000 by disease and famine, "year without a summer"); Wikipedia, "1815 eruption of Mount Tambora" (about 4,300 m to 2,851 m, about one-third of its height, VEI 7, caldera 6 to 7 km, at least 71,000 deaths in total); Wikipedia, "Mount Tambora".
Animation drawn in code; narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs).
